19.0.s.en: (1) Slaughtering the heifer and gathering its ashes

19.0.0.en: An ordinance of the law: that is, a rite and order that must be followed in what is to come.

19.0.1.en: A red heifer: that is, the color of its whole skin is red, with no spot on it, nor even a hair of any other color. By red is meant the light brown that is the well-known color of cattle, as Esau said to Jacob about the color of the lentils (light brown), "Feed me with that same red pottage" (Gen 25:30). The Lord commanded Moses and Aaron that the offering that would be set apart for the sacrifice of purification must be a heifer of red color, which the children of Israel were to seek out and bring to the Lord. The second condition, besides its color, is that it be perfect and without blemish, so it is not sick, nor does it have a visible defect or any other color. The third condition here is that it not have been used for plowing or field work, nor have had anything carried on its back.

19.1.0.en: Eleazar the priest takes the heifer, and it is slaughtered by him or under his eyes outside the camp. Then he takes some of the heifer's blood and looks toward the door of the tabernacle, while outside the camp, and sprinkles the blood seven times. The blood, of course, points to the atonement for the sins of all the people, and the seven times to the perfection of this purification. The red heifer is slaughtered outside the camp because it is a symbol of the uncleanness of sin.

19.2.0.en: Her dung: this is the remains of food in her bowels.

19.2.1.en: The Lord then commanded that the heifer be burned entirely, like the burnt offering or the sin offering, but outside the camp and not on the altar of burnt offering.

19.3.0.en: The priest, whether Eleazar or those who follow him in the later generations, takes three things that carry symbolic meanings and casts them also on the fire that consumes the slaughtered heifer. These things are:

19.3.1.en: 1- Cedar wood: it signifies incorruption, since it is not subject to decay.

19.3.2.en: 2- Hyssop: this is the herbal plant that signifies purification: "Purge me with hyssop, and I shall be clean."

19.3.3.en: 3- Scarlet: it signifies sin and forgiveness at the same time.

19.3.4.en: a- Sin: "though your sins be as scarlet" (Isa 1:18).

19.3.5.en: b- Forgiveness: because in its redness it signifies the blood of Christ who forgives the sins of the world.

19.4.0.en: As for the priest and the one who helped him in slaughtering and burning the red heifer, one law applies to both of them, namely:

19.4.1.en: a) He washes his clothes that were defiled by the blood of the sacrifice.

19.4.2.en: b) He also washes his body of the traces of the blood.

19.4.3.en: c) The two become unclean, so the priest may not approach the tabernacle or the service, nor may the person who helped him touch any other person until the evening of the same day of the slaughter.

19.5.0.en: A third person comes, after the priest and the one who helped him have departed and after the fire that consumed the whole heifer has gone out, and gathers the ashes remaining after the burning of the heifer. Jewish tradition teaches us that these ashes were ground fine and afterward kept in a safe place outside the bounds of the people's dwelling, that is, outside the camp, so that the people might use them through the priests when needed, that is, when one of them became unclean by touching a dead person, for example.

19.5.1.en: Kept for the water of separation: that is, the ashes are kept dry, but when they are used, some of them is mixed with water to be sprinkled on the unclean person. This water is called the water of uncleanness, although it is used for purification.

19.5.2.en: A purification for sin: the heifer is considered here a sin offering because it was used for purification from sin.

19.6.0.en: The man who helped in gathering the ashes also becomes unclean until the evening.

19.6.1.en: These ashes are a law and an ordinance that continues always, because of man's constant need for purification, whether for the Jew by origin or the proselyte from among the strangers who are not of the tribes.

19.6.2.en: The red heifer as a symbol of Christ:

19.6.3.en: There is no sin that does not need atonement or purification, and the sin of touching the dead came to signify the transmission of sin by contagion or association; in every case there was a need for purification. Here the law of the red heifer came, carrying many meanings, the most beautiful of which is that it is a direct symbol of the atoning work of Christ in cleansing sins.

19.6.4.en: 1- It is red: pure red is rare and distinctive among cattle, like Christ, who, although He resembled us in kind through the Incarnation, has no equal in the purity of His red blood, which did not bear our original sin.

19.6.5.en: 2- Without blemish: this is also a condition of the burnt offering, and Christ alone, of all the sons of men, is the one to whom this applies.

19.6.6.en: 3- Never yoked: that is, like Christ, who did not bear the yoke of sin, but bore on the Cross all our sins.

19.6.7.en: 4- It was burned entirely: in this is an indication of the perfection of Christ's sacrifice and of His complete sufferings.

19.6.8.en: 5- The cedar wood was added: the addition of cedar wood, which does not decay, is a clear reference to the Lord Christ, of whom David prophesied and said, "Neither wilt thou suffer thine Holy One to see corruption" (Ps 16:10).

19.6.9.en: 6- The priest was the one who offered the sacrifice of the red heifer and slaughtered it himself, and Christ offered Himself as a sacrifice on the Cross for the whole world.

19.6.10.en: 7- The red heifer was slaughtered outside the camp, and Christ also was crucified outside Jerusalem.

19.6.11.en: 8- The priest sprinkled the blood of the red heifer's sacrifice toward the house of the Lord, and Christ was hung on the Cross and they lifted Him up toward heaven to satisfy the Father and reconcile us with Him.

19.6.12.en: 9- The ashes of the heifer were mixed with water to purify the unclean, and Christ by His death on the Cross gave us the water of Baptism to save us from the evil nature and cleanse us from every sin.

19.6.13.en: 10- The ashes of the heifer lasted a long time, and the sacrifice of Christ also lasts forever, so He gives His Body and Blood to all generations.

19.6.14.en: 11- A little of the heifer's ashes purified every unclean person, and the smallest part of Christ's sacrifice, that is, His Body and Blood, purifies and satisfies every believer in Him.

19.6.15.en: If Christ suffered outside the camp to cleanse us from our sins, do not be troubled if others neglect you, or wrong you, or drive you away from them, for they did all this to your Lord Christ. Endure, confident of God's help that upholds you, and you will also experience His presence with you, and He will comfort your heart.

19.7.s.en: (2) Purifying one made unclean by touching the dead

19.7.0.en: The dead body of a man: this is mentioned here to distinguish it from touching the dead body of an animal.

19.7.1.en: Whoever touched a dead animal was unclean until the evening, but here whoever touches a dead human being becomes unclean for seven days; the continuation of uncleanness for seven days is an indication of the seriousness of sin and the necessity of being cleansed from it.

19.8.0.en: For this person the law of his purification must begin with the priest sprinkling on him some of the water of purification, which is called the water of uncleanness, on the third day ... and he repeats this action on the seventh day also (v. 19). But if he is negligent and does not come forward for purification on the third day, the seventh day comes upon him while he is still unclean. The spiritual meaning is that the seven days here signify the fullness of man's lifetime: time, however long, does not blot out man's iniquity, but repentance and the blood of Christ in the sacrament of the Eucharist alone blot out iniquity, which the purification on the third day signifies, in addition to the fact that the number three signifies the Resurrection of Christ and the seven days the seven sacraments of the Church.

19.9.0.en: Defiles the tabernacle of the Lord: that is, he defiles the camp in which God dwells in the midst of His people.

19.9.1.en: But if a person treats the law of his purification lightly and remains unclean, he is considered to be despising and scorning the house of the Lord and the whole purity of the people. The spiritual meaning is that the person who sins and does not come forward with repentance and the sacrament of confession before God becomes a transgressor not only against himself but against the whole Church, so his sin is multiplied many times over. Therefore the punishment in this verse is severe, as the sentence against him is that he be cut off from his people, that is, put outside the people, so that he is deprived of his membership in the people of God, and the judges may sentence him to death by stoning.

19.9.2.en: Beloved, if God in His mercies is longsuffering toward sinners until they return by repentance to His embrace, this does not mean laxity and indifference. The merciful God is not lax about the price of sin either, because continuing in laxity means, sadly, making light of the sacrifice of His only-begotten Son, our Lord Jesus Christ.

19.10.0.en: In these three verses is an enumeration and definition of the ways in which a person may become unclean by touching the dead, and the obligation of his purification. They can be listed as follows:

19.10.1.en: 1- Everyone who was in the tent of the dead, or entered it, or touched anything in it, and indeed every open or uncovered vessel, that is, without a cover, also becomes unclean; this is a symbol of the senses that are not disciplined and not closed against evil.

19.10.2.en: 2- Even if a person is in the desert or in the open field and touches one slain, or an ordinary dead person, or the remains of a human bone, or touches a grave, he becomes unclean.

19.10.3.en: The law of uncleanness is applied to the unclean person as mentioned in (v. 11): seven days, and of course the purification begins on the third day as explained before. Whatever the cause of the dead person's death, whether in a tent, that is, sin working in him gradually, or slain with a sword, that is, sin working in him suddenly, or a man's bone, that is, an old sin. For death is unclean because sin is its cause.

19.11.s.en: (3) The law and steps of purification

19.11.0.en: The steps of purification for one who has touched a dead person can be summarized in the following steps:

19.11.1.en: 1- This work must be done by a clean man, for it is not reasonable that one who is unclean should perform the purification, since the blind cannot lead the blind. In this is a beautiful teaching for all servants of the Church and its leaders: the one who teaches and guides must be pure in conduct and clean in conscience, so that he may be able to lead others.

19.11.2.en: 2- The clean man, who may be the priest himself, takes a little of the ashes of the burnt red heifer in a vessel and puts water on it, and also takes a bunch of the hyssop plant and dips it in this water and sprinkles the tent and all the furnishings, the bedding and the vessels that are in it.

19.11.3.en: 3- The sprinkling includes also all the dwellers of the tent who were present at the time of the death, and whoever touched the dead, or touched a dead man's bone, or a grave (v. 16).

19.11.4.en: 4- This sprinkling is done twice, on the third day and on the seventh.

19.11.5.en: 5- On the seventh day, after the sprinkling, the one who was unclean comes and washes his clothes and bathes, and becomes clean at the evening of the seventh day.

19.12.0.en: In this verse is a repetition of what came in (v. 13): whoever makes light of this law and the water of uncleanness, that is, the water of purification, is not sprinkled on him becomes a cause of uncleanness for the whole people, and therefore his punishment is severe, for this person is taken outside the camp and sentenced to death by stoning.

19.13.0.en: A perpetual statute: a permanent ordinance and a continuing law.

19.13.1.en: As for the one who was clean and sprinkled the water of uncleanness on the unclean person, he himself is considered unclean until the evening, and at evening he must also bathe and wash his clothes. In this is a beautiful reflection for our spiritual life: the servant, the guide and the priest who hears the sins and troubles of his people may be affected, even a little, and "become unclean" by what he heard, so he too must lift up his heart in prayer for his own sins and the sins of the one he heard, or for the sins of his people if he is a priest.

19.14.0.en: God affirms that sin is like a contagious disease, quick to spread and reach another. Everyone who was unclean because of touching a dead person and then touched another passes the uncleanness to him, and he in turn needs the water of purification. The spiritual meaning here is clear: a person must keep away from the wicked in order to preserve himself and his salvation, for being influenced is possible, and many people have lost their lives because of bad friends.

19.14.1.en: My beloved brother ... we must care for those who are far away and call them to Christ and the salvation of their souls, but set limits for yourself in mixing with their circles, lest you slip toward them instead of lifting them up to Christ. There is no one who is not affected by the surroundings around him, so beware lest evil enter your heart. The death of Miriam and Aaron and the water of Meribah

20.0.s.en: (1) The death of Miriam and the people's murmuring over water

20.0.0.en: The wilderness of Zin: it is an extension of the wilderness of Paran toward the northeast, and lies south of Canaan. As for Kadesh-barnea, where the people stayed and set up the tabernacle, it is on the border between Paran and the wilderness of Zin (map 1). The congregation of the people moved according to the Lord's command to the northeast and settled in Kadesh. The omission of the year in this verse made some commentators believe that it was the first month of the third year, while others thought it was the first month of the fortieth year. And Miriam the prophetess died in that place, and it is known that she was the elder sister of Moses.

20.1.0.en: Water in desert regions is always scarce, even when rain falls, and the people were accustomed to drink from natural springs or from wells they dug. Perhaps because of the difficulty of the rocky ground in the region of Kadesh they were not able to dig, and therefore the people chided Moses, that is, they protested and murmured against him, saying that our death with our brethren who went before us and died in Sinai would be better than what we are in now.

20.2.0.en: After the words had been addressed to Moses, the people also pointed the finger of accusation at Aaron with him, saying that the two of them were the cause of the people's destruction because they had brought them to this place where water is scarce. The people forgot that Moses and Aaron did not move except by the Lord's command by means of the pillar of cloud and the pillar of fire.

20.3.0.en: The people continue their protest and accusation that they had been deceived by coming out of the land of Egypt, where there were the Nile, greenery, shade, and abundance of water and food, in comparison with this barren desert, especially since until now they had not seen the promised land, which flows with milk and honey and abundant good things.

20.4.0.en: As Moses and Aaron, the faithful servants, were accustomed to do when troubles increased, they took refuge in God, and went to His house, that is, the tabernacle of meeting, and bowed down, humbly declaring their inability to find a solution and apologizing to God for this murmuring.

20.5.0.en: The Lord commanded Moses to take his rod and go toward a rock, perhaps one fairly high and with a distinctive shape so that Moses would recognize it, and to gather with him all the congregation of the people and speak to the rock, and it would bring forth water ... This differs from God's earlier command to strike the rock that was in "Rephidim" (Ex 17).

20.6.0.en: Moses rose from the ground and took his rod and prepared to carry out what God had commanded him.

20.6.1.en: We learn from the life of Moses, the faithful servant, something important: when great troubles occur, and the storms that Satan stirs up, we have no way out except to bow down, pour ourselves out before God, and pray with persistence, confident that God does not send away empty those who seek Him, and He will solve all problems, for nothing is impossible with Him.

20.7.s.en: (2) The water comes out and the punishment of Moses and Aaron

20.7.1.en: Despite Moses' great meekness before, and his endurance and breadth of heart, here we find him as if he had exhausted all his patience. He gathered the people before the appointed rock and addressed them angrily, saying to them, "Hear now, ye rebels," asking them whether water could come out of this rock?! Of course, by human logic, water cannot come out of rock, for it comes out of springs or wells, as is well known.

20.8.0.en: Moses lifted up his hand with the rod and struck the rock, while in the same state of anger, and thereby violated God's command, who had commanded him to speak to the rock and not to strike it. And because of the intensity of his anger, the divine inspiration shows us that Moses struck it twice and not once. Although this angry action was not according to God's goodness, God brought forth a large quantity of water so that all the people and also their livestock could drink from it.

20.9.0.en: God was angry at the disobedience of Moses and Aaron to His word, for He had wanted to perform a new miraculous work before the people, namely that merely speaking to the rock would bring water out of it ... But Moses' anger and his striking of the rock hindered the work of God, and this is what God expressed by His saying, "to sanctify me," that is, you prevented the people from sanctifying and glorifying My name by this action of yours. Therefore God's punishment of Moses and Aaron was severe and decisive, as He declared to them that they would be deprived of the land they had long yearned for and would not enter it with the rest of the people.

20.9.1.en: Moses' anger deprived him of entering the Promised Land, and the Holy Bible declares that "the wrath of man worketh not the righteousness of God" (Jas 1:20). So do not justify your anger, but offer repentance and apology for it, first to God and second to the one with whom you were angry, and God will have compassion on you and forgive you your sin.

20.10.1.en: As a conclusion to the preceding events, the divine inspiration declares that this was the story of the water of testing, when the children of Israel tested the Lord by their murmuring, their complaining, and their doubting of God's care for them; yet God showed His glory and His power when He brought water out of the rock and gave drink to all His people.

20.11.s.en: (3) Moses' conversations with the king of Edom

20.11.0.en: Edom: this is the name of Esau by which he was known, and it was applied to his descendants, who increased and became a people with a king. The people of Edom dwelt in the mountains of Seir, which lie between the Dead Sea to the north and the Gulf of Aqaba to the south, that is, on the border dividing present-day Jordan and Palestine (map 3). Map (3) shows the route of the people during their journey beginning from Sinai, and Kadesh was west of the land of Edom, and therefore the people had to pass through it to reach the land of their inheritance. Therefore Moses sent some of his men to the king of Edom, saying to him, "Thy brother Israel," that is, we are the descendants of Jacob, the brother of Edom, and we ask you to allow us to pass through your land, especially since you know very well the hardships that befell us, whether in Egypt or after coming out of it.

20.12.0.en: These three verses carry the summary of the message that Moses' messengers carried to the king of Edom, and its elements can be summarized in the following points:-

20.12.1.en: 1- They began by presenting their earlier history and referred to the humiliation they suffered in the land of Egypt, in an attempt to move the heart of the king of Edom.

20.12.2.en: 2- Making clear that God had not forgotten them but brought them out with a strong arm and a divine arrangement beyond human imagination, when their humiliation grew intense and they cried out to Him.

20.12.3.en: 3- The request to pass through the land of Edom.

20.12.4.en: 4- The promise that this passage would be a peaceful passage in which the people would not touch anything belonging to Edom: they would not eat anything of the fruit of their land, nor take even a little of the water, nor look with their eyes at anything on their right or left, but would go straight on their way to their promised land.

20.13.0.en: The answer of the king of Edom came severe and harsh, for he refused the request of Moses and the people, and even added to that by threatening them that he might destroy them with the sword if they tried to pass.

20.14.0.en: Moses did not despair, but returned a second time and addressed the king of Edom through his messengers in order to dispel his fears, saying to him, let us pass with our people, and we will even pay you the price of the water if we drink from your wells or your springs, for we want nothing but to pass on foot only.

20.15.0.en: With rage and hardness of heart, the king of Edom refused a second time the request of Moses and his people to pass through his land, and added to that by gathering his people and his men and going out to the border between the land of Edom and Kadesh, prepared for war if they tried to pass through his land. In view of this, Moses and the people decided to keep away from evil and not confront it, especially since God had not commanded them to fight him.

20.15.1.en: Here we learn from Moses, the wise leader, that it is not wise in any way to meet evil with evil, but we must avoid confrontation with it as much as we are able, for meeting evil with evil usually brings nothing but a greater evil whose price everyone pays, and a person loses his peace and calm, which cannot be valued by any other gains.

20.16.s.en: (4) The end of Aaron's service and life

20.16.0.en: Mount Hor: most probably it is the mountain known as Jabal Madurah, which is northeast of Kadesh (map 4). All the people journeyed in the northeast direction and pitched the tabernacle at Mount Hor on the border of the land of Edom, and there God spoke with Moses and Aaron, telling them that Aaron would not enter the land that God had given to the people because of his rebellion against the divine command at the incident of the rock and the water, but would be "gathered unto his people," that is, would die as his fathers.

20.17.0.en: God continues His speech with Moses and commands him to go up to the top of the mountain and take with him both Aaron and his son "Eleazar," and there Aaron takes off his garments, which represent the high priesthood, and Moses puts them on "Eleazar" his son, who would become high priest in place of his father, while Aaron's days come to their end and he follows his fathers in the hope of the redemption and coming of Christ. The taking off of the high priest's garments and the clothing of the new high priest with them became a Jewish tradition for many ages.

20.18.0.en: Moses did exactly what God commanded him, and indeed Aaron died after Moses clothed Eleazar in his father's garments. Perhaps the people saw this scene, and this means that Mount Hor was not a lofty or high mountain, and after Aaron's death Moses and Eleazar both came down to the people. Jewish tradition mentions that Aaron was buried on the same mountain on which he died.

20.18.1.en: And Aaron's death was on the first day of the fifth month in the fortieth year after their coming out of Egypt (ch. 33:38).

20.19.0.en: As for the people who saw this event and witnessed the death of their high priest, they grieved greatly and mourned for Aaron for a whole month, in recognition of his labor with them and his service to them.

20.19.1.en: Without doubt Moses and Eleazar were deeply affected by the death of Aaron ... who supported his brother first before Pharaoh of Egypt, second in the Exodus, and third in his priestly service. But Moses did not surrender to his sorrows because of his brother's death, for he still had work to complete before God and a mission not yet finished; and we too must grasp this lesson well and not let our sorrows disturb us .. but always lift up our hearts in times of hardship, asking God for help and support.

20.19.2.en: We also learn from the life of Aaron that however long a servant's life in his service, a day will come when he leaves everything, whatever his responsibilities; therefore the aware leader and faithful servant is the one who is concerned to teach, hand over, disciple and train others, so that the service does not stop or fall into confusion, and only the humble leader does this. The bronze serpent and the victory over many kings
